entry.title: The Era of Product Engineers is Here | Laurie Voss
entry.content:
As I continue to look for work in this poisoned industry, I've tried to pay attention to what folks in the space are saying about it and determine if I really need to consider stepping out. Laurie's interview highlights quite a few things that I found poignant:

  • "only white guys can afford not to go to college": I never went to college because my family didn't understand it (non-English, uneducated immigrants) and because of how my high school life went, I was immediately written off. Software engineering as a trade saved me in some capacity.
  • "the thing we found in senior engineering has become central to the job": this means that there's no longer any space for on-the-job training of the skills that would have normally skilled people up; there's negative incentive to have folks become articulate into these roles
  • "we don't know who the big players are": the AI vendors. They literally are the biggest players; operating like Stripe when it comes to understanding which smaller businesses are rising or falling since we're submitting all of our information (the new data/product) over to them.

There's a very different perspective that folks who are invested in this industry's bubble not happening within the next five years versus those who might be a bit more like me, who doesn't completely mind the death of the role (at least in its capital hoarding way) but is concerned about the lever that's been released in favor of letting statistical models drive business decisions.

It is a lot easier to be optimistic about generative AI when you're:

  • comfortably employed
  • have sonority that allows them to move through interviews faster
  • have already been in the industry for at least twenty years (or ten)

This makes them ignorant to the day-to-day[1] that they never have to engage in; making these optimistic stances reductive. What's more likely to happen is what's happening now: increased ramps on layoff cycles as technologists are submitting their knowledge to machines that'll produce a lot more closed source technologies (there's no point of contributing to the commons - there's less of a competitive advantage if you can throw Jev, Muse and Gemini at the monster of a codebase). This is even mentioned in the podcast - the rise of "(generated) personalized software".

I suggest you read more of Laurie's stances so you can see the gap (or rather the executive perspective) in how this is and how this works in real life (no matter what Markdown files scanning spreadsheets show you):

  • https://seldo.com/posts/do-ai-enabled-companies-need-fewer-people/
  • https://seldo.com/posts/ai-has-torched-the-market-for-junior-programmers/
  • https://seldo.com/posts/we-are-all-product-engineers-now/

Then come up, watch that video and tell me how much money, thought and concern is actually being put into junior software development (none), employment stability (none) and the durability of the career path that is software engineering (very little). Feeding into the hype is no different that investing in the wet labs!

  1. If not ignorant, it makes them less likely to take the sentiment of the thousands of people around them at a lower value. It makes it easier to devalue people they could even call peers into EINs that are plugged into aggregates of information from https://fred.stlouisfed.org/. ↩︎

entry.title: Dorsey for the People
entry.content:
Ever since listening to the first episode of Revolution Social with rabble and Jack Dorsey, my opinions on Dorsey have slightly changed. I didn't understand - not fully - why he allowed the sale of Twitter to Elon, but that episode talks more about it (tl;dr: capitalism wins over logic every time). That capital has been one he's been sitting on but as of late, he's been funding a lot of projects that are anti-cenorship, something I'm adamant about, which is different from moderation, something Dorsey inherently disagrees with as a concept (to my understanding, at least global moderation; selectively imposable moderation like ATProto is more of his speed, though he had angsts with it being built in).

Across the globe, state-enforced internet blackouts have become a primary weapon against protests and independent journalism during political crises. Beyond silencing dissent, these measures serve to block real-time documentation and evade international scrutiny of official misconduct.

The next time someone tells you that the Internet isn't real life; point them to this article. If they're still apathetic, they don't need their opinions to be taken that seriously.

This report is compelling. The now-fascist Indian state has been attempting to silence protestors for some time now. I've only learned of the state of India by way of the amazing work of Arundhati Roy. But having a government attempt to block access to code that is legally free has a bad way of precedents — imagine if the United States' president passed an executive order blocking any code that helps promotes critical race theory?! Wikipedia, Google, the whole Internet would be out!

Bitchat reached an all-time high of 430,000 daily active users in India on July 26, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Between July 20 and July 26, India accounted for 74% of the app’s global downloads.

If this is not a market signal that the app is ripe for revolutionary (if not counter-state insurgency) action, then I don't know what is. Those paying attention will most definitely be looking to see how they can expand this with things like mesh networking or WiFi repeaters to boost up what's available over Bluetooth. Dorsey going as far as posting the government order on his old platform (ironically, I don't think he did it on Primal, the Nostr equivalent of Twitter/X) took me out.

As someone building a social network for readers, especially those who want to read radically, I can only imagine that it's a matter of time before this reaches other places and becomes a new battlefield of sorts.

entry.title: Yeah, 16% of people are reading. We're cooked.
entry.content: According to this piece, reading rates in America have collapsed - fewer than half of adults read a book in 2022 (which - eh - I feel like this is hard to assess), daily pleasure reading fell from 28% to 16% (which is both real and wild; if reading is dead then folks are going to be just told what to think) across (and this hurts me to repeat) every age, gender, and education level, even as total words consumed explode via texts, posts, and feeds. Reading built and freed the modern mind (logic, sustained attention, rational analysis), and its erosion is reshaping cognition, politics (Trump as the first "postliterate president," whose rhetorical style suits oral culture and yet challenges a truly democratic one, even those with a farce of an existence as that of America), and democratic institutions that assumed informed, literate citizens. Generative AI now threatens writing itself - which is how people figure out what they think - risking the loss of deep thinking and independent judgment, making the literate era look like a brief anomaly between the oral and digital ages. This has been hard for me to assess with even my own heavy use of generative AI but damn does the prospect of folks just not giving a fuck anymore is scaring me.

entry.title: Erin's giving apps a meaningful story
entry.content:
Erin Kissane is launching "Cloud Atlas" — an interview-based guide to the apps and projects emerging on the AT Protocol/Atmosphere, intended to make decentralized social media infrastructure more legible to people interested in alternatives to centralized platforms. This is something I haven't seen done from the outside — developers of these apps and services tend to be their own marketing departments and PR teams but this isn't (solely) that.

The human texture and qualitative specificity of projects in the Atmosphere are as interesting to me as any set of technical and design specifications could possibly be. Interesting for their own sake, and also for the ways they’re shaping each project’s current state and its likely futures. I also believe in just getting out there and gathering foundational knowledge. There's value in offering classification systems even when they're provisional and even when they’re only one among many. I read a lot of oral histories and interviews and human-textured research from older social movements and periods in technology that inflects my understanding of the world now—the ACT UP oral history project that kept me sane in during the Covid Tracking project, the very human testimonies of the Combahee River Collective, even the (delightful) work that came out of the early stumbles of the Worm Community System. I like to think that if things go even halfway well, the work we’re all doing to make new online social systems legible will help in the present and be a useful ship’s log for the people who come after us. Understanding what we’re trying do—and why—will matter later, is the bet.

This is the kind of work that keeps projects both alive and afloat in the minds of many. I'm extremely curious to see how Erin pulls this off and kind of hoping that my own project, Livtet gets to be in this party.

entry.title: Dissent's Sizzling the Block with this Summer Issue
entry.content:
Patrick Iber opened up this issue in an almost prophetic way with the editor's opening:

The semiquincentennial celebrations planned by the White House will not be a demonstration of unity. They will celebrate the domination of one part of the country over the other. Donald Trump’s 250th will be a carnival, complete with a barker-in-chief, attempting to sell the idea that the United States is winning like never before. Outside of MAGA-land, there will not be so much celebrating. It is hard to cheer when Trump will insist that the festivities are made into a reflection of his glory.

This section was immediately highlighted because it couldn't have been phrased any better. I do wish that the lawsuit to stop the event from happening landed but relying on the legal system to enforce any sort of justice is like asking CitiBank nicely to return the money they stole from the Haitian National Bank — a joke all around. I disagree with quite a bit of what Iber continues on to say because it clings to this idea that we can just refactor the "bad parts" of the American project and lean on "small-d democratic control, not big-D Democratic control" to fix the ailments of this project. The first essay after the note operates like a palette cleanser because it's way more honest and direct about the place that the United States has in its evolution as a global power that's attempting to drag the rest of the world down with it.

The American Revolution in Global Retreat

This essay prompted a few posts I made on Bluesky as I was reading it on my flight to ATL Monday evening[1]. I found it a great way to reframe the way other countries try to get the favor of the United States in their own political ventures - like India and Indonesia:

In his 1949 speech to the U.S. Congress two years after Indian independence, Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru called the American founders the “torchbearers of freedom, not only for this country but for the world.” Indonesian President Sukarno opened the famed 1955 Bandung Conference of Asian and African states by highlighting the anniversary of Paul Revere’s midnight ride, which informed settler militias of advancing British forces prior to the battles of Lexington and Concord. Sukarno declared the Third World’s anticolonial struggle to be the culmination of a “battle which began 180 years ago” with “the American War of Independence, the first successful anti-colonial war in history.”

During the twentieth century, U.S. independence became a symbolic touchstone for many communities in the Global South that would have been excluded from that revolt. It stood for the idea that all people have the right to govern themselves and to fundamentally change the conditions of their own societies. For all the flaws of the American Century, its great attraction was the degree to which economic, political, and cultural life seemed to exist in a dynamic relationship with the will of its changing people. Above all, it was this relationship that gave world-historical significance to the events of 1776 for outsiders. Rather than a local political conflict unleashed by restive settlers, the long-term engine of American renewal meant that an eighteenth-century spark could be linked to an unfolding global story of human freedom.

The focus it brought to the global conversation: that the American Revolution was the grandest and most noteworthy is refuted by C.L.R James, as mentioned in this piece. If the mission of independence, of freedom - as described by Thomas Jefferson and F.W. Reitz - is tied to one's authority to "exterminate the brutes" and invoke "manifest day", it makes sense why then the ceiling of political understanding that Black capitalist and celebrities have are that of house Negro-esque ideas: staying as close to whiteness and mimicing its talking points (despite the cementing in history of cultural production it might have brought - the cost is intellectual and communal damage for the profit of a few):

The State Department may have sponsored jazz tours, but in the era of Coltrane such art often remained inflected with global anticolonial solidarity in ways that challenged any easy Cold War purpose. These oppositional connections certainly did not disappear, but by the twenty-first-century age of Black billionaires like Jay-Z and Oprah, commercial creativity seemed to fit far more comfortably with both American capital and power.

I'm still working my way through this issue but best believe I'll be following up; it's been full of bangers so far.

  1. Namely this one but also this one because of how my ethnic and national identities tend to collide (or be selected for me by an observer) and the way that spoken language and accentuation plays into that (and what conversations folks assume I'm allowed to partake in). ↩︎

entry.title: 'I Love Boosters' Is a Black Marxist Movie
entry.content:
I enjoyed every moment of I Love Boosters. From Lakeith Stanfield's attempt to woo our lead character to the literal heightening of contradiction that led to a global workers' revolt — this is the kind of media that makes plain the difficulty of the people who are ignored and belabored for the comfort of the upper class. It focused on the production of fast fashion, the industry that's the underacknowledged child of the industralization of attire and the elitism of what it means to be "in style" (Haute couture, for example).

I'm glad that they took time to explain something every baby Marxist (or serious leftist, that is) has to understand: dialectical materialism. The most ridiculous moment of this is quite literally a scene of .. well, sex but second to that was a moment when Taylour Paige's character was blasted by the "situational accelerator" that works as a way to exacerbate conflict of a situation or to deconstruct every element of material that produces the object. One example of this was the aforementioned sex scene - which was very abrupt - but also her donning a suit that heightened her senses:

This movie is one I'm adding to my personal DVD collection and will throw on when I want something to remind me that you can make a funny, zany and educational film for the left all in one go.

entry.title: 'For All Mankind' Is Great Until Season 3
entry.content:
This will have spoilers for the TV show, For All Mankind.

I've been enjoying my binge watching of this show. My friend's wife suggested it and I've been hooked since. There's points of the show that make my leftist brain itch too much but it's part of the narrative of what makes America America - its jingoistic, racist but ever-curious, persistently curious and overly ambitious goal to get ahead by any means necessary.

Now Season 3 is where things get very interesting. Due to the work of the public sector, the private sector is able to capitalize on the development of space travel and end up competing with two national superpowers to make it to Mars. At this point, the show enters full-on fantasy (one - folks are going to Mars and we elected a woman President who's bad at hiding that she's gayer than a chaise lounge). We also get to see the exceedingly annoying hubris of a man be the guiding factor of NASA finally be matched by his inability to be a decent role model for men leading to him being indirectly cucked by his best friend's son.

The science of the show is very cool including things not yet fully proven or has failed in the past like helium-3 and underwater rocket launches. I also learned about the deep-faking technology they used for the Reagan and Nixon era. It's an interesting show because it's clearly science fiction but also is toying on the edge of literal fiction. I will say though - this show both reinforces the tropes of how the Soviet Union depicted themselves in yesteryear and has me way more curious on watching older Russian television to see how they were actually depicted. At times, it feels like there's some directive by the State Department that all TV production studios are required to produce a uniform depiction of what Russians look like. I feel like it was one of the cheapest parts of the show.

With all my misgivings, I think this show is great. I'm planning on finishing it!

entry.title: It's Biased Bullshit all the Way Down
entry.content:
Well, well, well - this is a bit of a doozy. Not shocking or surprising, but a doozy nonetheless. This report from Stanford highlights quite a few things:

  • AI hiring tools are helping folks break the (weakly enforced) law around hiring bias.
  • Blackbox (proprietary) systems help shield companies from this bias-as-a-service.
  • "Black applicants are the most likely to be adversely impacted: 30% of Black applicants apply to at least one position that demonstrates adverse impact against Black applicants." For tech companies, this number is definitely way higher.

I wrote about my frustration, despite having a tenured background, in reading a book on "tech resumes" and on the job hunt itself. I don't believe folks are entitled to a job - I do think that if we're not going to provide durable and reliable employment, that we need to have society provide a social net with all of this excess capital such that we don't end up criminalizing them for things that jobs provide like the means of paying for rent, buying food and at this point not being sick. That's the silent part of the idea of labor: we're not entitled to security but we are guaranteed social exile (by homelessness) at best and prison at worst when forced to make moves undesirable to the "job makers."

A bit extreme from the realm of tech workers - especially the highly paid ones like myself (perhaps when you're not floating two families) - but it's the truth of the system that we silently enable by not doing anything about it. I do not expect people whose job is largely to speak on the greatness of industry (Lenin was right about https://www.economist.com/, as a subscriber for two years now) to seriously address this. That's a problem because they become the canonical voice of industry and there's a class of peers - kinfolk or not - who use them as a barometer of how good the industry is going despite reported issues being held up elsewhere.

entry.title: Revolution.Social
entry.content: Over the last few days, I've been speed running (at 1.75x) a podcast by Evan called https://revolution.social/, which is a bit of a build-up to what his company is building; a "permission-less" social media network. I am a bearish person by trait and do not move under the notion of "assuming positive intent" — that has to be earned. That had me struggle with some of the insight that Evan provided during his podcast due to what I'd label as a very utopian, "moun nan mond li a" (people only of his world), perspective on the future of social media. Due to his career, access and social circles, he's been able to host a genre of folks to talk and probe questions about their perspectives on social media and how it's impacted them as well as a bit of a biographical dump for each person. It's also preventing him from seeing the locked-in levers of comfort that he sits in and how it still reinforces the systems (and not create a system of dual power) on the systems he claims to be against. To a degree, I wonder if the social ties (and access) is more important to him than the actual principles he espouses — that's problematic because that makes it easy to be sold.

entry.title: Ghost is a Concrete Success Story
entry.content:
Ghost is demonstrating the power of independent media being able to fight in a landscape of venture capital capture and corporate consolidation. The shape of the organization running Ghost is a non-profit, which is more common for open source projects to take on; another example of the lack of the need to run to the explicit for-profit model to make change.

The excuses I tend to see about the "lock-in" of using Substack lean on the very things that Ghost provides — even before this release. This has me believing that, in some cases, publishers — be it large or small — don't mind cohabiting with Nazi content. The access they gain in these circles seems to more important than the integrity of what they report on. I've seen a few publishers, namely Taylor Lorenz, call this call to leave Substack a form of virtue signaling, from those who are in her comments about it[1]. I have a bit of a qualm with the concept of digital virtue signaling but I can see how folks who aren't funding you but wanting to give you executive direction as a way of "yelling from outside of the club".

Looks like there's less reason to stick in the NaziStack, though!

  1. I don't necessarily follow her explicitly for journalistic purposes (or in general). It came across my feed on Bluesky. ↩︎

entry.title: Open Source eInk is a Step Towards Healthy Technologies
entry.content:
I've been paying attention to changes in this company's attempt to create open e-paper technology. I'm quite a fan of the concept; it makes technology less encroaching on one's attention and helps with reading in low light and low power situations. In a world where everything is racing to (and passing!) 4K imagery, it's great to see folks focused on keeping our eyesight and focus intact.

Unfortunately, I don't have an immediate development use-case to purchase such a device. I do hope this finds its way into those who are making things for folks!

entry.title: Communal Instructure is the Path
entry.content:
Drew makes a lot of good points in this piece regarding self-hosting. In a way, we see sprinkles of this when public universities keep e-mail infrastructure for those who are alumni. In a way, even looking at the postal office and its ability to support "virtual" mailboxes, allowing folks to operate public proxies to store information. The point Drew makes about libraries being critical in this aspect of infrastructure building is important too: public libraries are designed to provide us with the basis of this. It would require more funding from the state to make it an actuality in a few places:

  • Libraries to operate as local data centers, optimized around local power demands and made more efficient, versus our current approach of data farms the size of cities that require equivalent means of cooling and powering.
  • Each state to provide an ISP to allow folks to pick between the commercial offerings and what's available in the private sector. This isn't difficult in theory; we have this today with broadcast television, although this is losing its backbone of funding.
  • A public specification for durable computing and storage that one can use for holding this. This is probably the "extra" part of this but having a specification for the baseline of "home compute" can help people build with reference hardware and equalize the playing field for access. This can allow folks to borrow equipment to host but keep the actual storage of data to themselves by means of portable storage (like a USB drive)

Hazel wrote a thread on Bluesky that I agreed with - in some parts. The subsitence farming model worked - to a degree - in places that are allowed to exist communally. The closest form of that that we can get to today would be via policy that does some of the things I'm thinking about above (or in some form that enables people to allow themselves a hybrid network setup).

This conversation is great because it's not one in isolation. There's a hope amongst Black archivists to help build out a means of connecting one another that can be almost as resilient as the ways we've always kept our stories and experiences alive. Conventionally, this was kept by way of oration: we'll tell our stories to one another, pass it down with song, imagery and the like and that'd be part of our archival traditions. Instagram and Facebook have upsurped this for my generation and the need of us to return (or introduce) a system that honors the people who contribute to it is one we need to look to investing in.

entry.title: So We're Just Going All In on Microsoft's AI for Code
entry.content:
This thing opened up with something that I couldn't relate to: putting questions, big or small, into a generative text tool to get an answer from. I understand that Google, Microsoft and Apple are educating as many people as possible that this is an okay thing but we don't have to keep parroting it.

Anyway.

I recommend walking through the results: the demographics, the disabilities markers and the like. I was a bit shocked to see Neovim on there but it is a pretty flexible editor. As expected and dictated by market dynamics, Microsoft's tooling — through GitHub CoPilot, ChatGPT and the like, all dominate in usage and deployment. When you can make it free and use said free input to refine their work, it begins to pay for itself — according to economist/trickle-down "theory" logic. There's also a bit of a bias in that most people only have used one coding "agent" and you can't filter against that[1].

Something I expected was that it'd be predominately the language that's the most difficult to document that'd be at the top of this list. I believe that languages that have baked in documentation have less of a need of discovery for tools like it. That and the difficulty of building for the Web puts that language higher on the list of "how the fuck do I do this" (the whole point of generative code tool). Accessibility to the runtime is another factor, perhaps, but negligible. More folks need to use TypeDoc; my $0.10 (ignoring tariffs and stagflation).

Half of the use of refactoring use is either because folks can't read the code or they want to rename variables (which folds into the first, IMO). That explains why the happiness marker seems way more optimistic than it should be. The note on "strong consensus" of AI integration into workflows is notable as well as folks mentioning increasing productivity. Does productivity means more time spent "doing things" or less time getting to something "productive"? Additionally, removing the neutral option to be a 4-opinion split regarding AI existential risk might have leaned it towards more of a "no" just on the fact that developers tend to underestimate things. The reaching AGI part is just embarrassing, tbh.

This ending with a AI-promoted-in-young-classrooms note told me what I needed to know about this survey: a soft means of reaffirming Microsoft's tool integration into the lives of developers (since we collectively refuse to leave the ecosystem) by means of labor automation.

Thank you, next.

  1. The magic is so wide, it probably makes it statistically irrelevant but it does beg a question of inspection: if it's only CoPilot, then does the market space really breed competition? Can you compete with a company that keeps inhaling everything around it? ↩︎

entry.title: Free software is for folks who enjoy the terminal
entry.content:
Provocative title aside, Tante's derived point about free software being optimized for those who are comfortable for hackers is astute. It's definitely a big factor as to why you don't see folks in BestBuy or Target asking clerks, "does that come with Linux pre-installed"? Part of the experience is the expectation that folks will and can "do it themselves". Organizations have tried to combat this[1] but cultural and corporate expectations of computing in the United States lean against things that allow for anti-degradability, repair and autonomy — this is the country of maximal convenience and minimal engagement, after all, if you can afford it. Folks might want to point out that we've recently reached a point where all of the states have introduced bills for right to repair. The word "introduced" is important here, as it's hopeful (but personally unlikely) to this become a federal mandate once enough states go for it. This is in part of a push to reduce the economic burden of constant production and will end up creating a market where companies can forcefully sell their parts with only OEM blessings. Apple's an expert in this kind of work.

In the case of software, it's less important. Because of the reforming of the Web browser into the now-fabled "omni operating system layer", the underlying operating system seems to matter less and less to "casual" users. They can open up their preferred-by-suggestion browser, Google Chrome, and get to their places like Facebook, Reddit, or what have you. What does software freedom matter to people who just want to connect with family, watch a movie or play video games?

Ironically, a lot. In the same way that the average American isn't versed in the Constitution that (kinda) governs our lands and a bit more understand (recently) how and where the people who make up our governing bodies move, folks wouldn't know that it's more important to keep your hardware as long as possible to offset the impact of its production[2]. That becomes difficult as some folks note how even the most expensive and revered companies forcibly encourages device replacement. This makes them more money in the long term instead of investing in methods that can expand device life from the perspective of the device owner[3]. In the case of software, we can see that we've entered the golden era of forced upgrades and non-backward compatibility as a service.

Open source developers have a chance, especially if they develop for the expensive and American-centric Apple ecosystem, to build escape hatches for their software such that folks aren't tied aggressively to the Apple walled garden. There's little incentive to do so for the same reason that folks don't ask questions when they go into Target: it's "easier" to go with the script. Apple doesn't make it terribly easy to use their services outside of their ecosystem, so the fault isn't entirely in the hands of developers: once again, it's the means of production.

  1. Remember WUBI? God, that was a hell of a time. The fact you could sidecar it with Windows XP is a big contributing factor to how I began with Ubuntu in those days. ↩︎

  2. The cost of pollution and ecocide when it comes to developing technology is mostly in the act of manufacturing. You can read about this in The One Device in the chapters where the author travels to each location of mineral extraction and development for Apple's iPhone (and other products). ↩︎

  3. One approach here would be allowing for simpler replacement of batteries as they atrophy, adaptable cables for use and the like. The technology was available but Apple notably was more focused on controlling the aesthetic appeal of the device over anything else. ↩︎

entry.title: Do you remember how to search for things?
entry.content:
The video's creator warns early that this is a "old man yelling at cloud" kind of video and I think they do themselves a disservice with that. The ability to search for information is a skill on decline and that's a big "winning" attribute of technology: to remove as much labor as possible from humans, regardless of the task. Need a house cleaner? There's an app for that! Need to dig your heels into generational racist neighborhood watch policing? There's multiple apps for that! Looking to determine which women to prosecute based on their ovulation cycles? There's a plethora of apps for that. Surveillance aside, technology is an amplifier of the underlying behaviors we have. It can also introduce new ones that supplant others that we've developed along the way — like searching.

The video goes on to explain how despite this, YouTube still provides a way out for folks. I avoid using the YouTube app directly and use [FreeTube][1] to follow folks I'm wanting to stay up to date with and to open any YouTube links as a whole. Most of the money made from YouTube isn't from ads either; it's largely paid members and views (which are tied together; you're more likely to get the former when you can juice the latter — an extremely equitable platform)[2].

  1. https://freetubeapp.io/ runs in most places, thanks to the power of Web browser engines. ↩︎

  2. According to Hootsuite, this is the case. This justifies my personal move to places like Nebula; where I can seemingly both support creators and watch ad-free content. Like how we used to. Want to learn about Alfred Hitchcock's white woman fetish? ↩︎

entry.title: Democracy Now: Cory Doctrow on Tech Workers
entry.content:
Cory's interview with DemocracyNow came across my reader this morning and I was glad to hear someone speak on the internal class struggle of tech workers: especially software engineers. One only needs to look for a reference as to how technology under capitalist society works very marginally to improve the lives of the few who can afford it and cannibalize the labor of those who keep it up. In this case, he speaks to tech workers who are beginning to encourage the picking away of their own colleagues by way of AI.

I've clipped the part that more tech folks need to internalize and understand with their advertising of corporate AI:

He continues on tangible approaches of protest that workers can engage in. I have waning hope in tech workers wanting to engage in this due to the heavy internalized liberalism of workers as a whole. They find that the business of the company is more important than any sort of harm (perceived, actualized or otherwise) for the sake of soaring to the top of Hacker News or getting a blessing from some venture capitalist firm. One day, computers will be less important.

Watching that after watching an interview with Simon Willison on The Pragmatic Engineer that endorses the means of destabilization that's described above. Ardent folks for genAI will see this as a reach and I remind them to read anything by anyone who's written extensively about the harms that have come to pass and will continue to pass as this continues to roll around.

entry.title: When the Empire Turns its Tools Within
entry.content:
The concept of colonialism, the expanding of control of a people, their environment and culture, is foreign to the American populace; at least those who are "citizen-native"[1]. This article is co-authored by the same authors of Data Grab. It's a succient explainer of what many folks have been chided as "extreme", "ridiculous" or "outlandish" for: the core purpose of the companies of the Silicon Valley collective is to absorb, quantify and monetize as much information as possible about everyone who touches their systems. It defeats the breadth and scope of privacy that one could advocate for[2]. I'm appreciative of this article. I'm also confident that the folks who need to read this won't or will allow their corporate alliances to prevent them from understanding that they aren't a comrade or even a customer to these companies: they're a cog.

  1. These are people who either have immigrated without any sort of duress from land seizure or capture directed caused by a Western force. ↩︎

  2. Folks will declare that things like end-to-end encryption is a viable stopgap and many privacy advocates more wiser than I have confirmed that. With the recent capitulation of Apple to the UK, it's clear that if and when the 5/9 Eyes collective need such a tap; they can (and will) create it outside of the press: it's already happened. ↩︎

entry.title: Framework Is Giving Folks Options
entry.content:
The CEO opening with a statement that "we're the only company that can announce a product and it look the same each year with applause" made me smile but Apple has definitely locked in that title. To their credit, as a Framework 13" owner, these machines are built such that you won't have to keep replacing it over and over. Because of things I'm working on the side, I immediately noticed a few mentions of companies in the hardware. Namely, Honeywell; a household brand that keeps you cool and also working on literal energy weapons — once sci-fi shit, but now they're in the new Framework 13 boards to keep them cool. Cool?

They mentioned that the stock shipping versions will come with a Microsoft CoPilot button and the DIY versions will be without. I understand that Microsoft has the weight of manufacturing control when it comes to this but I do wish that, in a different world, more PC makers would push back against Microsoft in some capacity.

Curiosity and Ambition

I was extremely eager to see the new desktop release by Framework. I have no need for such a device — I already own enough machines reflective of my class in society. The novelity of a small PC, especially one small enough to port around is attractive — as someone who needs to have a separate machine when doing presentations or tech work in the community, this would help out quite a bit.

The "AI" advertising is lazy. This is not Framework's fault but it's potentially clear that AMD is pushing hard to get more "AI"-centric cards into the world, perhaps to challenge NVIDIA (in some capacity). And it seems like this is the only approach for boards available as all of them are branded "AI". In a different world, I'd be more interested in a more generic board (which doesn't feel too impossible — look at the laptop board offerings).

Marketing language aside, it's clear that this is something that they can still push to tinkerers since the casing for the PC is relatively standard: with their experimental RISC-V board, I'd be eager to see them consider developing an equivalent to allow for truly open computing - from the silicion to the software.

Tangentially, I do loathe the adoption of the "elevated keynote" thing that the tech industry adopted from Apple. I can't give Apple the full share of blame — Microsoft and IBM did this in the past. At the end of the day, they all want you to buy — regardless of need.

The 2-in-1 12" laptop is a really interesting product offering. It's extremely niche of a idea — and it's definitely something that can help folks escape the Apple ecosystem if they're aggressively locked into the portable computing landscape. I would love this as my introduction machine; I have a now-defunct Dell XPS 2-in-1 that got a lot of use in its tent and tablet mode for reading and watching media.

Things I'm Interested In

I'm personally considering getting the following:

  • The purple translucent bezel for the Framework 13": I already have the solid one and my machine's dominantely this color so it feels apt.
  • An Ethernet expansion card for personal projects around wired systems.
  • A 32GB RAM stick; I've been great with a solo 32GB for virtualization work but I'd like to give my host machine more breathing room as I work on things, like media editing and game development.
  • A bigger battery because my battery life over the last two years has taken a nose dive. I do use this as my primary machine and I rarely shut it down (it's usually in suspension, docked or completely off when I travel).
  • The 2.8k display also feels like a necessary bump with the media and game work I'm doing as well.
  • A hat because my hair's finally short enough that I can wear caps and I like the logo.

Some of these parts will lead to me having spares, which the community tends to have plenty of. When I do retire this PCB, if not because of wear, I'll turn it into a HDTV receiver or donate compute cycles for some sort of open computing project.

entry.title: Cory Doctorow Talks about Enshittification
entry.content:
One thing I find about authors; good ones, is that they can give a good talk. Doctorow's one of them. While I have gripes with his work on Chokepoint Capitalism, it'd be disrespectful to ignore the research and accessibility of the book itself. This talk opens up with a quick retelling and explaining as to how finance began taking control of then-utility-centric companies became more degraded experiences over time.

People have mentioned that he's a good orator and I see why — again, I attribute this to being a good writer. He swiftly highlights the coupling of state and corporations working to milk every ounce of value from people and manufacturing even more value by crafting more value from commodifying every aspect of our lives. As someone, for a very brief moment, who played into the idea of the quantitative self, this was something I bought into. It wasn't an explicitly selling of myself but it was a public validation of the mass quantification of behavior that we see companies now sell as a new flagship feature, as opposed to making things like replaceable batteries or alternative application distribution channels.

Cory's video from the year prior is also good and it's clear that he picked up exactly where he left off.

entry.title: Is School the Place to Find Oneself?
entry.content:
Jose Vilson's reflection on the role of how education, as a marker of status, of identity and of self-direction gave me a bit to think about. I'm not the popular type of Haitian; I don't folllow any organized religions, I don't have any form of heavy accrediations and I don't optimize myself around making a lot of money. For many migrants and children thereof, there is a pressure to assimiliate heavily into what conservative Black America deems as the "way forward": buying our way to respect. However, Vilson breaks away from that a bit here with the focus on education: one of the career paths that's routinely discouraged because it's not as profitable as being a doctor or lawyer[1].

His reference to teachers being the vanguard of society is something I resonate with and it comes as the antithesis of the aforementioned: instead of an obsession with building a golden calf today, we work to ensure more stable and fertile lands for the future. It's not to fall in the path of longtermism but to understand what things we are doing today that we have seen yesterday that'll make tomorrow more challenging for those who are going to be in our positions.

What his cousin said is something I'm considering heavily, provided life and resources align; on the idea that school can be a place to return if one is seeking guidance or feeling lost in life. Perhaps.

  1. The exception to teaching in this capacity would be if you were a high-ranking (thus more highly paid) official within academia. It's less about what you do for the children and more aobut how much you get paid. ↩︎

entry.content: As much as I understand some folks for wanting computers to reduce the amount of rote tasks we employ, I still can't shake the pending nature of violence that's happening with the reallocation of funds in favor (or rather, at the whims) of corporate propganda that this is the best use of capital in society. I've mentioned it a few times on Mastodon, but we've (re)entered a point in society where people who could be either replaced (or at best, defunded) by genAI are strongly picking up the tools of their potenital demise. entry.title: Mainstream Tech Journalism Works to Maintain Tech's Corruption
entry.content:
I have no intention in reading Swisher's book. I make it a personal policy to read things that work to expand my understanding and after listening to an episode of Tech Won't Save Us where the author of this article was invited to speak, this book doesn't seem like it'd do so. Something Edward mentions her is how I felt about other journalists when it came to handling things like the situation of willingly platforming Nazis:

The long and short of it is that Swisher is not a good journalist—or, framed more generously, that she thrived in an industry with remarkably low standards for which we are still paying the price. For decades, tech journalism and criticism has primarily consisted of glowing gadget reviews, laudatory profiles, and reprinted press releases, all of it colored by Silicon Valley’s self-aggrandizing vision of itself as a laboratory of a brighter future.

This is effectively what outlets like The Verge, TechCrunch and other flowery outlets of the industry have become (or always were). It's fair to say that these organizations are tightly beholden to what's allowed to be printed; but that's not necessarily an excuse for those who can (and have) gone independent to continue beating the same drum. I briefly got chastised online for announcing my unsubscribing from a journalist who effectively did this. It took them to privately address them to finally have them shift their stances[1]. There's really one way this happens and Edward says it plainly:

This is a compelling narrative only if you ignore every available fact.

I've written a bit about my disdain for companies like Apple that take advantage of overseas labor and have an operating capacity that mimics that of the more abusive companies in the tech industry, a mantle now taken up by Elon Musk. However, in my personal experience, I found that things like this matter less depending on one's investment into a company. For example, I've been told that I should focus more on Google or Microsoft instead of Apple because of the value they provide. It strikes me as a narrow perspective to note that when I have in the past (and currently still am) critical of both of these places. Edward mentions, in the same podcast episode, about the importance of listening to the people whose labor craft these companies; the contractors instead of the C-suite, the manual labors instead of the marketing teams. By directly and uncritically consuming the party line of a company, you're doing their work for them[2]. That's what folks like Swisher and (from my own reading and review) Casey Newton enable. We need to end the worship of the executive, consider business journalism to be no more than tabloid material and focus on people and their needs. Swisher's note of being the "tech whisperer" makes her nearly as responsible for stroking the egos of these men[3]:

The first thing Swisher did after learning about this was to call up Yahoo chief executive and cofounder Jerry Yang. “You need to get them off your platform,” she warned, before turning to the audience to note that “I did not often warn companies, but I had seen this so many times before that I could not keep it to myself.” Other potential ethical lapses abound: Swisher advises Rupert Murdoch not to invest in Vice Media, Mark Zuckerberg calls her late one night for her feedback on an essay he is writing, Page asks Swisher for help writing an essay extolling the virtues of Google—including its long-ignored “Don’t Be Evil” commandment—and Elon Musk asks Swisher for her thoughts on what to do with Twitter shortly after acquiring it.

If Elon Musk is calling you for advice — you're not someone I can take seriously. Edward ends this with something that reminds me of something Anil Dash has written about the ultra-wealthy and their need to exist in a bubble:

I use “we” loosely because Swisher’s intended audience is not you or me, but instead those with power: she writes about and for them. Over the course of a long and storied career closely reporting on the tech industry and its titans, she has aped their motions, sat at their dinner tables, drunk their wine, gone to their weird parties, played with their baubles, repeated their lies, and offered them counsel. Swisher may style herself as Silicon Valley’s critic laureate, but she’s much closer to the court fool.

  1. The underlying issue being that, in this big age of 2024, we still have to have people relearn why it's not good to give space to bigotry. I imagine that a level of para-sociality is at play here as well as a level of false optimism: that folks will eventually see their way. This is a largely privileged (and secure) stance to take. It's so due to the lack of that being the case in the industry, demerits the efforts of journalism that challenges the envelope and works to trivialize the issues that sparked discourse to begin with. ↩︎

  2. A bit of a callback to a frustration I had about wrestling with the wrong ideas. ↩︎

  3. Which is more evidence of how woman can play into the egotistical side of patriarchy; as researched and documented by bell hooks, specifically in the case of Black people. ↩︎

entry.title: The Mindset of the Wealthy Is Inverted
entry.content:
Dash opens this piece with level setting about his position of wealth[1] and balances that with his own background. He grounds it with the notion that rich people are willing to potentially forego a tight bond with their families in order to accumulate wealth. This is historically accurate[2]. It's short but the closing point about the storage and accumulation of money versus the ability to direct a stream of money is something that stood out to me:

Put more cynically, you can't exert control over something if you've already stopped paying for it.

This can explain a number of things:

  • Why tech CEOs are incapable of not aligning with right-wing stances on finance, labor and ethics: to do so will remove the control they have over people lives like the ability of them to support themselves. Elizabeth Anderson notes this in Private Government as a way to control a worker's autonomy (emphasis mine):

Exercising autonomy — directing oneself in tasks, no matter how exacting and relentless they are — is no ordinary good. It is a basic human need. No production process is inherently so constrained as to eliminate all exercise of autonomy. Elimination of room for autonomy is the product of social design, not nature. It is not merely "unpleasant" to be denied a rest break when one needs it. When some authority denies it (as opposed to when some natural constraint prevents it), the restriction demeans one's agency.

This is what folks like Bezos enabled at his warehouses or Kalanick (and the Doordash, Taskrabbit and Lyft executives) with their misclassified employees by denying them benefits and simple human dignity.

  • Why we see more tech companies more willing to shoot down collective organizing: doing so forces workers (at worst, into a state of fear and apathy, and at best) into a place of defending executives who routinely will put the needs of the ultra-wealthy over them.

Dash's point on repositioning the perspective is a good starting point to begin challenging what and what the rich are aiming to do. However, there's more that we need to do: especially around becoming more horizontally aligned in what we need workplaces to model and who's even considered a worker. Things to address in another post.

  1. As a former CEO and now executive at one of the largest Internet companies and a history of being in places that few can be, it's understandable to assume that some level of stability and wealth has accumulated. He even notes this to manage to remain living in New York; despite the rising costs and tides. There's a reason why I haven't managed to move back. ↩︎

  2. For example, many of the wealthy African slave holders, including one who had a plantation in now-named Montecello, had no issue with infidelity despite being a God-fearing man and routinely raped his foribly enslaved captives ↩︎

entry.title: The Inherent Right-Wing Nature of Billionaires
entry.content:
Anil writes briefly about the nature of billionaires and tech venture capitalists from his experience around them. Folks who seem to imagine themselves as the new Rockfellers and the ilk, with near-full control over industry and policy when it comes to tech. Tech, both as a concept and an identity (to some), effectively moves to their whim. He concludes mentioning his faith in those working outside of this insular realm to help counteract their actions.

I'd believe one of those forms of action to be in the form of collective organizing: where workers recognize and pool their labor-power to both reign in power and reclaim it from those who control our ability to support ourselves. However, it's important to peek a bit closer at what this means. The once-glamor child of the tech industry and social networking space, Jack Dorsey, has taken a pretty hard turn towards the right. He's gone from attempting to help foster the open social Web with some initial funding for BlueSky but now has become the silent and invisible contender in the space of cryptocurrency work under the moniker, TBD. Quite annoying to search. I do believe that solely focusing on these people, the VC QAnon, is doing the same amount of unncessary narrowing of focus as we saw with Donald Trump and focusing solely on him as the source of American issues.

We need to be more honest and broaden our understanding of why this industry is so easily capable of producing people like this. It's not because money corrupts. One of the reasons is that it's extremely profitable to work against the needs of people. A prime example of this shows up in Malcolm Harris' Palo Alto; a working history in the development of the "Silicon Valley" as he recounts how tech is yet the expansion of how this country demands production at the cost of people here and abroad. As Netscape grew, computer manufactures worked with state governments for fast track access to handle the fabrication of the personal computers and ship it back to the United States at a premium to citizens. This is now the model used by every company: from Apple to Samsung, as described in Dying for an iPhone.

Yes, these former nerds now billionaires are on one and the systems we use everyday that we are committed to upholding further entrench their power. That's as long as we allow it to. Reclaiming control of our lives can take on many forms, from labor organizing to progressive lobbying to direct action. But we can't keep it as just the off-shoot of a few folks wanting control over everyone else. We also live on this planet — on this Web.

entry.title: When people in the movement replicate the power structures
entry.content:
Karla's piece finally came on my radar after reading about the grift of the founder of Raheem AI. I did not expect this to come out such of an organization, but as I've mentioned to her on BlueSky in response, this is a subtle growing (if not already metastasizing) issue within leftist coalitions and how we deal with money. I can't lie, someone using organizational funds to blow $50,000 on ridesharing is wild to me: was he paying for himself and the community? We'll never know.

Karla's point here is something that resonates with me (emphasis mine):

For as much as the left — which I’m defining loosely for the purposes of this writing as a coalition of people fighting for MRC Democracy — would deny we were culturally impacted by that movement, we have taken up a few of its toxic cultural tendencies. A very human thing to do when you are surrounded by toxicity. I am most concerned with the use of domination as a primary tool to get what we want and even as a form of entertainment. This toxicity has infected our friends, families, communities, and institutions. It is a poison that will silo us and have us reject coalition at every turn.

That bit about using domination as a form of entertainment is really deeply ingrained in so much of how we approach life: we're exposed to it as a concept since our early youth. Compeition, though seemingly healthy for growth, in my opinion, plays a big role in this, when it spirals to be mainly a competition of the "biggest, best and boldest". Something that's a core component of Silicon Valley's culture (and what American culture is at large).

The four points Karla makes around the forms of domination give me echos of experiences I've seen (and have engaged in) online across the Fediverse and Twitter[1]. I also see examples of it in how conversations unfold about who and what is allowed in one's perception of the "greater community".

Another point she makes reminds of something I'm learning in "No More Heros": the idea of having a spokesperson of your toxic stance (emphasis mine):

That being said, when those tradeoffs are made, we tend to villainize each other. We also tend to elevate someone who is either a grifter or seeking attention who says we can have everything we want without pain or sacrifice.

A singular human is never the reason big sweeping glorious change happens. Equally, a singular human is not how big, life-destroying pain happens — unless you have THAT much power and your blast radius is just that wide. This means that making those tradeoffs cannot be how we come to write each other off. I don’t mean a sustained pattern where the same people are paying the cost of tradeoffs over and over isn’t immoral and shouldn’t be called out. We should. I mean boiling every situation down to — they made that tradeoff that impacted me and that means they must be evil. I am not saying this tool shouldn’t be used either — I find it quite useful for known bad actors like white supremacists trying to change Overton windows. But not everything is that, some things require depth of conversation and negotiation in a diverse society — or as sociologist Tressie McMillan Cottom calls them — thick conversations.

One point of emphasis that I do appreciate is her highlighting of this angle of a singular point (or person) being the cause of something (notwithstanding a sort of gravitional pull). This is something media (social or broadcast) leans into a lot due to the simplification of the message. It's a lot more digestable of a sound bite to understand something like Donald Trump being the source of racism in the United States versus parsing the last century[2] and the racism that has now become "normal behavior".

Karla's point on the use of identity as a potential anchor that prevents deeper conversation is something I have to admit I've subscribed to (and am aggressively working to stop):

Using the label does not get us to the change we seek, it calcifies the conversation — freezing it in place because even talking about it somehow makes us immoral. Naming the behavior that is upsetting us and how it is influenced by our social biases gives us more room to learn in community. It is not the strategy for the far enemy that I’m talking about, it is the needs of coalitions I’m concerned about. I understand many of us have not had language for this kind of specificity but the shortcuts we used to take are not going to work in a world where leaders of color have consequential power.

This is why I've spent so much time over the last three years reading more from folks who've been doing this before I came to be (let alone moved into this space). It's a responsiblity to use this position and space wisely[3]. Her final point is the one I'm working on the hardest and was what inspired my post on the wrong ideas:

I get what I want or I take all my marbles with me is not a way to create democratic governance. It creates smaller and smaller groups run through authoritarian norms. That [accustoms] people to authoritarianism in the small ways, not prepares them for shared power in the big ways we will need to build necessary muscles around.

This is hard for me because I believe I needed to draw very clear lines in the sand as to where people can bring me and where I was willing to do. But I forget that it's sand: that these lines can be redrawn, that people are not single-issue and it's possible to work across lines. Don't get me wrong, this isn't easy. It's sorely needed when it comes to how the Left handles and approaches money, for example, but it's a process in relationship building that's needed if we actually want to build power.

  1. I'm on BlueSky but my engagement with it is lower due to a smaller community of folks that engage with me. I'm not able to see things go down unless the algorithm feeds it back to me and the people I follow. ↩︎

  2. It's not common knowledge, for example, that the modern from of Jim Crow ended in 1975 and that we've transitioned into something folks call Jim Code; a more exportable and replication-friendly form of the same forms of oppression but now applicable over class as well. ↩︎

  3. This is what I was trying to explain to Aral some time ago but I do think a level of xenophobia is potentially at play and prevented him from grasping what I was saying. I also don't believe I communicated it well enough — no one is perfect. ↩︎

entry.title: When Pacifism and Anarchism Meet: Fighting the Highest form of State Violence
entry.content:
Pacifism as a concept perplexes me[1] so this reading of the role that these two concepts, anarchism and pacifism, had in contributing to the anti-war movement was interesting. However, this review has made some statements that I can't disagree with. It opens up strong:

Violence is not all the same. Context matters. There’s something much worse about violence when it’s perpetrated by or with the tacit acceptance of the State. It’s not just that governments and their allies in the capitalist class and the patriarchy have more resources, more weapons, and fewer ethical qualms about killing than most. Beyond these obvious assets, they can hide behind the veil of legitimacy that the State (allegedly) offers them. Hitler, George W. Bush, and Derek Chauvin may not have a lot in common personally, but all committed their crimes under the reasonable presumption that the social and political order sanctioned such behavior.

This statement is bold and can cause a knee-jerk reaction depending on who you are. If you're accepting of American violence, putting George W. Bush wouldn't make sense until you consider that his war led to three million innocent Iraqis dying over a lie on weapons of mass destruction. Chauvin had a twisted agenda[2] but would be considered a villian to most Americans, especially because of his figure, the mask falling.

This book is interesting but not compelling enough for me to engage. I respect pacifism as a concept but I have yet to see a concrete example of it working outside of the West[3]. How do you suppose the Sahel belt practice pacifism, for example? This is a reminder, for me and readers, that solutions aren't (can't!) be universal. But that doesn't mean that they shouldn't be taken (if viable). The review continues, however, with an indication of post-World War II America:

Repeatedly in Akst’s book and the contemporary writings of people like Muste and Dellinger, pacifists made the inconvenient point that in the name of winning an all-out war against Hitler, the U.S. was adopting many aspects of Hitlerism itself.

The astute reader who expands the perspective to be beyond the West will note that it is valid. This was also a time when the US government and its allies also were manipulating so many African and Asiatic countries in attempts to maintain their control over the land. The reviewer seems to have a particular ignorance towards anything that non-white folks (sans Martin Luther King Jr and Bayard Rustin) were doing. They write, at the time, "the new radicals of the 1960s never [finding] a way to engage the American labor movement in their struggle, or generate an alternative for working-class people in their increasingly complacent and ineffective mainstream union establishment". Questions like "who were able to make up union representation at this time" come to mind. Bayard Rustin was also a very prominent figure for labor as a high ranking representative for AFL-CIO; who, around this time, gave way for police to be more concretely recognized as workers. No one is perfect.

  1. There's a level of both security and sacrifice to be a moral witness willing to threaten one's own life in favor of the collective. It's the ultimate form of moral upholding; the choice to never take a life. I find it hard to wrangle with given how violence itself is almost endemic to human nature. I imagine that depends on what you believe to be "human nature". ↩︎

  2. Chauvin's approach, while targeted, still didn't get the result of exposing institutional police corruption. It's hard to wrestle with this because such institutions exist to cause violence. And for Black people to exist in them require a level of soul murder and disassociation from Black solidarity that I can't align with; a different form of violence. ↩︎

  3. In before a mention of Gandhi, the English didn't have the resources to fight off natives at a number of 200 to 1. It wasn't pacifism but a decision made to not be made into a fool in front of the world. Gandhi also has … complications; from my understanding. ↩︎

entry.title: Facebook's Threads Preps to Introduce Advertising
entry.content:
Facebook is an advertising company. It makes a considerable amount of money from advertising[1]. This is not to be shocking but a warning. The fact that someone has managed to flip it in the app is indicative of whatever soft attempt that they had with "joining the Fediverse" could introduce them scooping up the open social Web as part of a larger advertising network beyond their walls. App developers of the Fediverse need to brace themselves for this.

The head of product mentioned this intent. If anything, we need to get more serious about enabling some means of "creator sustainability" in the Fediverse; being open isn't enough now. The infection of surveillance capitalism into the open social Web has been here.

  1. They say that they're "reliant" on the such in their most recent earnings report. ↩︎

entry.title: AI Photo Editing Brings Propaganda Production to the Masses
entry.content:
I understand (to a degree) how photo editing works. I also (to a even lesser degree) understand this for AI photo editing. But now Google, being the alleged arbitor of truth and knowledge has given society a tool that can effectively rewrite history if folks aren't paying attention. And we're really too tired too because we, as a society, are continuing to accept empty promises as policy notes.

The examples of the imagery shown is scary and yet to be expected in a piece like this. But it shows Google's disregard for launching such a product. The teams invovled will get promotions, down to the ICs and we'll see more instances of abuse via image editing rise. The need for markers of undoctored images will rise but it'll be a cat-and-mouse raise as anyone with enough drive will find a way to break through this.

This will now make me extremely distrustful of random imagery and I really don't like that. There's so much to be provided with the power of imagery (and also to be considered in its role of mobilizing people) and now we've been given a form of naplam to the whole space.

entry.title: Anarchy, the Rise of the early FBI and the Mexican Revolution
entry.content:
This book review immediately introduced me to quite a bit that I had to look up. Before we had the FBI as it stood today, we had the National Bureau of Criminal Identification in 1896. It was seemingly formed in response (if not to help track) the rise of anarchism in the United States, specifically after the assassination of President McKinley. I didn't know a president outside of JFK was killed and for it to be specifically an anarchist is huge, given the way America's strength against dissent is heavily curtailed today. All of this seemed to be at the strong urges of President Theodore Roosevelt.[1]

What freaked me out is how this was effectively instrumental in the formation of the modern day police force. As mentioned in Prisons By Any Other Name, there's a history of Texan rangers attacking Indigenous people (who are the modern day ancestors of Mexicans). I quoted a portion about this on Bookwyrm, but below is what came to mind:

Volunteer police helpers also have a long history in the United States of facilitating Indigenous genocide. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, for example, the Texas Rangers chased down and killed Native people rumored to have attacked colonizers, and they lynched Tejanos, or Texans of Mexican descent. But the Texas Rangers were not actual police, military or even militia forces; instead, these volunteer vigilantes were essentially "community members" playing a collaborating role in policing and protecting newly arriving white colonizers.

It's truly horrifying to understand that the symbolism of that badge comes from a history of genocide on "American" soil. This review continues with the journey and assaults that the Magon brothers experienced during their efforts to liberate Mexico. Some motivations that pushed people were things like labor repression in copper mines in 1906 as well as the forced migration of Indigenous people to Yucatan - all around 1906. This ties in with the Brown Belt of Jim Crow like law (Juan Crow, as it's called) being pushed on Mexican Americans. It is disappointing but not surprising to see how a lack of development of sexuality and tolerance also led to the Magon's campaign — you'll have to check this out to understand more on that.

There's so much more that this article goes into. I really want to read this book! If there's one thing I don't know much about, it's definitely the rise and formation of Mexico and its development as a country (as well as those who fight for liberation within it).

  1. It sounded like he was afraid of dying after taking the highest seat in the land. What is it with people in power and being afraid of letting go of it? ↩︎

entry.title: Donors, Funding and the Left
entry.content:
This is another hit from the Fall 2023 issue of Dissent; following the previous one about the Supreme Court and union striking power. Money and the Left in the United States is such a sticky topic. This article does a better job than I can on explaining the situation specifically from the non-profit angle. It references a book I'm eager to dive in on the topic raised by women and femmes of color on the role that non-profits have in stifling grassroot movements. It goes on to mention that this process is a bit of a double-edged sword: without guidance, these organizations can't spend well. It seems like more often than not, "the disparity was especially apparent in coalitions, where funder darlings (often national organizations that claimed to be "connective tissue" between local affiliates)[1] contributed just the occassional meeting attendance, while low-paid organizers at base-building organizations worked more than seventy hours hours a week". This isn't sustainable and I can see why this kind of work turns a lot of people away by default.

Thankfully, this article does highlight some solutions that I agree with: bringing these people (funders) into spaces to have them understand the struggle at hand[2]. That way, the funders don't feel like they're doing charity but are direct partners in alleviating, if not eliminating, the problems at hand. I have some contention that's developed from something that reminds me of a post I've written on my approach to reaching folks on how the need to humanize funders is a missing component and it has me wondering, again, if I'm reaching the wrong people as "goals". This also runs into slight conflict with something I've been reading Kaba's book; the need to focus on the big picture of issues instead of working to organize for individual release in the case of prison abolition when we can. I think both are necessary and that we have the people to do it; it's all about mobilizing folks so we can plant both of these trees at the same time and bear the fruit for everyone.

All in all, a great read with some strong takeaways!

  1. This reminds me of Code for America's bridage network that was disbanded in 2023. The community was not approving of it in the community Slack. ↩︎

  2. The word struggle has a strong weight behind it that's tainted by class politics. I'm sure someone's written about this at length: I'll find it and link it from this site soon. ↩︎

entry.title: The Right to Strike
entry.content:
This piece by Veena Dubal for Dissent has been the longest read in this issue for me. So many moments where they've expanded on how, even despite Justice Jackson's work to highlight how striking is necessary for workers in a democratic society, the majority opinion is increasinlgy swaying towards corporate control. They include a quote from Sean O'Brien after the case of Glacier vs Teamsters that "people cannot rely on their governments or their courts to protect them ... We must rely on each other". This, despite being nearly a year old, is a good call to action for those interested or adjacent to organizing to understand that we, in the United States, are fighting a system that is inherently against workers at every turn.

As mentioned, wildcat strikes[1] are our strongest weapon. They demonstrate a truer form of workplace solidarity that'll be needed regardless of who takes office in January 2025. It's humbling to know that even despite the anti-worker and anti-Black presidental campaign (nee administration) of the 1980s and its push to reduce worker organizing, there's been growth. "According to the Economic Policy Institute, U.S. strike activity increased by nearly 50 percent last year — even as the percentage of workers represented by a union dropped one-third of a percentage point", writes Dubal.

If you're a worker, especially if you're in tech, the best time to get organized was yesterday. The next best is today. If you're able to come to San Francisco in October, there's a conference just for you.

  1. These are strikes that are either unconsidered unlawful or can bring heightened risk to the company or institution being striked against. ↩︎
